description: We are Team AETHER, exploring how Earth's extreme environments can guide future Moon and Mars bases. Using NASA imagery, planetary maps, and Perseverance rover data, we compare geology, temperature, pressure, humidity, and radiation across three worlds. Our interactive portal brings research, maps, and scientific charts together, while our Sparjon rover concept imagines safer exploration. AETHER turns Earth analog research into practical insights for choosing and preparing future human habitats.
summary: AETHER is our bilingual (English and Persian) interactive web app for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It compares the Moon and Mars with Earth analogues, meaning places on Earth that resemble a specific feature or condition on another world. Side-by-side interactive maps link features on Mars (such as Jezero and Gale craters) and the Moon to matching sites on Earth, including the Lut Desert, Atacama, McMurdo, Iceland and Death Valley. Each pairing explains why the places are similar and where they differ. A day-and-night temperature lab compares NASA MODIS surface temperatures for Lut with the Moon and Mars, and charts show real Perseverance weather data (temperature, humidity and pressure) and Curiosity radiation measurements. The project also presents the AETHER rover, a six-wheeled concept for the Moon and Mars that astronauts can explore in 3D and that converts into a temporary inflatable habitat. Built as a single HTML file with Leaflet, Chart.js and 3D graphics, it uses NASA Worldview, Moon Trek and Mars Trek. Throughout, it states its scientific limits: an analogue matches one feature, not a whole planet.
details:
What it does. AETHER is our bilingual (English and Persian) web app that compares the Moon and Mars with places on Earth. Its day-and-night temperature lab shows how surface temperature swings on each world: in Iran’s Lut Desert, NASA MODIS recorded surface temperatures up to 80.8°C; at the Moon’s equator the surface drops from about 390 K at noon to about 95 K before sunrise; and Mars swings by 80–100 K every day. Interactive maps link features on Mars (Jezero, Gale) and the Moon to matching Earth sites such as Lut, Atacama, Iceland, McMurdo and Death Valley, and charts show real temperature, humidity and pressure data from Perseverance and radiation data from Curiosity.

Benefits and impact. It helps students, researchers and mission planners see which Earth sites can be used to test rovers, equipment and astronaut operations for the Moon and Mars, and which conditions each site cannot reproduce.

Tools. A single HTML file built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Leaflet maps, Chart.js and 3D graphics, using NASA Worldview, Moon Trek and Mars Trek. It runs in any web browser, with no special hardware.

Creativity. It puts three worlds side by side, including live day and night temperature maps, and presents our own AETHER rover concept in 3D: a six-wheeled rover that converts into a temporary inflatable habitat.

Factors considered. Scientific honesty: Earth surface temperature is not the same as Martian air temperature, each analogue matches one feature rather than a whole planet, and the rover is a concept, not a tested design.
